issues.legal_issue: Publication of a controlled-area declaration in the official gazette makes the declaration effective even when publication of its contents in the required newspapers occurs later.
material_facts: A government declaration identifying a controlled area was published in the official gazette before the land was purchased or construction was undertaken.
The declaration’s contents were published in newspapers only later.
The affected landowners challenged enforcement on the ground that delayed newspaper publication left the declaration ineffective.
issues.conclusion: The newspaper-publication requirement was not mandatory in the sense that failure or delay in complying with it invalidated the declaration; the official-gazette notification made the controlled-area declaration effective, and the subsequent newspaper publication also fulfilled the procedural requirement.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 4(1) and 4(2) of the Punjab Scheduled Roads and Controlled Areas Restriction of Unregulated Development Act, 1963, publication in the official gazette declares an area controlled, while the direction that the declaration’s contents shall also be published in two newspapers is not a condition whose non-compliance nullifies the gazette notification. Sections 5(1) and 7(1) refer to publication of the notification under Section 4(1), supporting that construction. The Court distinguished Collector (District Magistrate), Allahabad v. Raja Ram Jaiswal (1985) 3 SCC 1 and Bhavnagar University v. Palitana Sugar Mills (P) Ltd. (2003) 2 SCC 111 because those decisions concerned land acquisition and its different statutory scheme and consequences.

predicates.appeal_challenges_controlled_area_enforc: The landowner brought an appeal challenging enforcement of restrictions on land treated as being in a controlled area.
predicates.gazette_declaration_published: The government published a declaration identifying the area as controlled in the official gazette.
predicates.newspaper_publication_delayed: The contents of the declaration were published in the required newspapers after the official-gazette publication.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenging controlled-area enforcement concerns a gazetted declaration whose newspaper publication came later, the declaration remains effective.

issues.legal_issue: Failure to provide adequate notice does not warrant relief from enforcement when notice was sent or affixed, the affected person responded, and the enforcement decision was reviewed on appeal.
material_facts: Notices directing the affected owners to stop construction were sent by post in some cases and affixed at the premises in all cases.
The owners learned of the notices and filed objections.
The owners were informed of a right to appeal, pursued appeals, and had their objections considered by the authorities and the tribunal.
issues.conclusion: The challenges based on want or inadequacy of notice and natural justice were properly rejected.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed notice in light of the record of service, the owners’ actual responses, and their subsequent opportunity to appeal and present their objections. In those circumstances, the notice arguments did not establish a basis for interference on natural-justice grounds.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_enforcement and notice_sent_or_affixed and affected_owner_objected and appeal_opportunity_used

predicates.appeal_challenges_enforcement: The affected owner appealed an enforcement decision concerning unauthorized construction.
predicates.notice_sent_or_affixed: The authority sent notice to the affected owner or affixed notice at the premises.
predicates.affected_owner_objected: The affected owner learned of the notice and filed objections to the proposed enforcement.
predicates.appeal_opportunity_used: The affected owner had an opportunity to appeal and presented the challenge to an appellate body.

issues.definition: In an appeal against enforcement, a notice challenge is rejected when notice was sent or affixed, the owner objected, and the owner used an available appeal opportunity.

issues.legal_issue: Construction or land use contrary to restrictions on scheduled roads or in a controlled area, without required permission, may be ordered removed.
material_facts: The affected owners constructed buildings or made access arrangements near a scheduled road, including construction within the restricted distance or access without prior permission.
The affected owners used agricultural land for a non-agricultural purpose without obtaining permission.
The construction or change of use occurred without the permissions required for the relevant restrictions, and the authorities ordered removal and restoration.
issues.conclusion: The authorities, tribunal, and High Court were justified in upholding removal of the unauthorized constructions; the enforcement decisions were affirmed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(1) of the Punjab Scheduled Roads and Controlled Areas Restriction of Unregulated Development Act, 1963 prohibits specified construction and access arrangements within the restricted areas beside scheduled roads and applies from the Act’s commencement. Sections 6, 7(1), and 8 restrict construction and land use in controlled areas and provide for permission; Section 12 addresses contraventions. The Court emphasized that the Act’s public-safety and planned-development purposes should not be defeated by technical pleas or official delay, and that public interest prevails over the private interest of those who violate its restrictions.

predicates.appeal_challenges_removal_order: The affected owner appealed an order requiring removal of construction or restoration of land.
predicates.construction_or_access_in_restricted_roa: The owner constructed within a restricted area beside a scheduled road or laid out access to that road.
predicates.required_permission_absent: The owner undertook construction or a regulated change of land use without obtaining the required permission.
predicates.agricultural_land_used_for_nonagricultur: The owner used land that was agricultural for a non-agricultural purpose without permission.

issues.definition: An appeal against a removal order fails when the owner undertook restricted road-area construction or access, or an unauthorized non-agricultural use of agricultural land, without required permission.

issues.legal_issue: A lease granted contrary to restrictions governing village common land does not confer a right to the land or a right to construct on it.
material_facts: The appellants obtained leases of land from a village panchayat.
The leases were granted contrary to the governing village common-land statute and its rules.
The appellants relied on those leases in challenging orders requiring removal of their constructions.
issues.conclusion: The leases conferred no right to the land or to put up constructions, and the appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the Punjab Village Common Land (Regulation) Act, 1961 and Rule 3 of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Rules, 1964, holding that leases made contrary to those provisions confer no enforceable right to the land or to construct on it.

predicates.appeal_challenges_removal_order: The lessee appealed an order requiring removal of construction on leased land.
predicates.land_leased_from_village_panchayat: The appellant obtained the land under a lease granted by a village panchayat.
predicates.lease_contrary_to_governing_requirements: The lease was made contrary to the requirements governing village common land.

issues.definition: When a lessee appeals a removal order concerning land leased by a village panchayat under a lease contrary to governing requirements, the lease gives no right to the land or to construct on it.
